topComments.author: jsmith45
topComments.text: While this does largely work, there are a few complications. The biggest one being power management, especially the cutting off of power to a specific port. If a host wants to cut off power to a 3.x device, it typically needs to know which 2.x port that device is connected to. The host internally can have some really wild mappings of 2.0 and 3.x hubs, controllers, etc, but the device tree or ACPI tables let it know exactly which ones are paired together for any port leaving the device. After that point it is assumed that the host can learn the topology from any hubs attached. The power management is tied to the 2.0 port. Unexpectedly splitting the topology could lead the host to instruct a hub to cut off power to the wrong port when trying to target a specific USB 3.x device. Also, if a hub indicates that a device is drawing excessive current, and there is nothing communicating on the 2.0 lines, there is a risk of the wrong 3.x getting blamed by the host, possibly showing a warning popup to the user with the wrong device name, or similar. This isn't to say this is always a problem, because it isn't but it is something to be aware of.

jobs.text: Those fucking rent-seeking hyperscalers took the internet away from you, and we’re going to give it back to you and to everyone. Web 1.0 was great - we had IRC, file sharing, third party chat clients. There were personal websites, forums. Flash was a format kids could use. Everything supported embedding and uploading. Websites actually had APIs and RSS. File sharing, FTP, MP3s, discs, owned media. Broadband brought our parents and grandparents online, but the shift to the non-technical majority created an opportunity to grossly oversimplify everything. Everything dumbed down into a pre-packaged product. Startups began turning their offerings into walled gardens. Platforms took precedence over protocols. APIs and access and data export went away. And then the rent-seeking began. The era of ownership ended. Corporate Memphis. Jesus Christ. We’ve rallied a massive community to build MIT/Apache-licensed alternatives to Adobe, Microsoft Office, Google Workspace, Autodesk, SolidWorks, Slack, Discord, Unreal Engine, OpenRouter, RunPod, and more. The goal is full feature parity, with code anyone can own, inspect, modify, and build on. We’re digesting second-class apps and platforms into first-class applications, libraries, and APIs with full MCP support. We’re distilling out the good parts, and we’re building the connective tissue that draws them together. 100% of the internet is going to be open source soon, and we’re going to force it open. Loudly. We have eight figures in run rate revenue, over 20M app downloads and growing. Our community is the best part, and it’s energetic like a wildfire. Everyone resonates with our mission. We’re missionaries, not mercenaries. We are going to slay the incumbents by being better. Our motto is Google’s old motto - “Don't be evil (tm)”. We’re a tiny team looking for strong engineers to own major parts of the product: desktop apps, lots of completely open source backend infrastructure, agent workflows, agentic app factories. Stack: Rust, a sprinkle of TypeScript/React, egui, Tauri, MySQL/Postgres, Redis, Elasticsearch, Kubernetes. Lots and lots of Rust. We’re systems engineers by trade, but we like to vibe code Rust. Did I say Rust? Rust. Rust Rust Rust. Maybe that's a filter. You have to be self-directed and independent. If you want to open source Salesforce with half your time, do it! If you want to work on Solidworks 3D printing applications, great! Writing music apps and DAWs? Go for it! Custom Discord/Slack clients for our custom, completely open source chat API and platform? Hell yeah. Our organization is flat, and we're going to go after everybody and everything. Everything you build here will be open source. We have no private repos. We can reclaim the internet. That’s our mission. Want to know more about us? Look up “Adobe ArtCraft” on YouTube / TikTok / your platform of choice. If this resonates with you, email hn@storyteller.ai with your Github, a little about yourself and something you’ve built. Write the sentence, “don’t take my RAM, Sam!” so we know you’re one of the good guys.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Can a conforming implementation produce an execution that is different from the logical deduction according to the standard?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: Consider this example: #include <atomic> int main(){ std::atomic<bool> flag = false; while(!flag.load(relaxed)); } IIUC, the program should never exit due to the control flow dependencies. That is, the program exits implies the loop exits, which in turn, requires that there is a side effect setting the flag to be true and the side effect doesn't happen after the value computation. The relevant formal rules are [stmt.while] p1 In the while statement, the substatement is executed repeatedly until the value of the condition ([stmt.pre]) becomes false. [intro.races] p10 The value of an atomic object M, as determined by evaluation B, is the value stored by some unspecified side effect A that modifies M, where B does not happen before A. The semantics in [stmt.while] p1 and [intro.races] p10, and the program exit are not observable behaviors in terms of [intro.abstract]; a conforming implementation only requires to emulate the observable behaviors. However, IIUC, control-flow dependency is a crucial part of reasoning about program behavior. If an implementation only needs to adhere to observable behavior, a conforming implementation could very well produce an execution completely different from the logically deduced behavior, as long as it does not manifestly violate the behavior specified in [intro.abstract]. In other words, if an implementation terminates the program in a way that seemingly violates [stmt.while] p1 and [intro.races] p10, yet preserves observable behavior, is it considered conforming? In other words, is it valid for a program that theoretically never halts to actually exit? Is behavior that contradicts theoretical deduction really what the standard intends? If a conforming implementation is permitted to produce an execution that would exit the main function for this program, what's the meaningful of the semantics of the abstract machine we used for deducing the behavior of the program?

stackOverflowQuestions.title: Put legend keys on top and bottom of colorbar
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I have plots with gradient colourbar, that the numbers don't really mean anything, just the relative amount does, so I replaced the tick text with descriptions. However, ggplot2 puts legend text next to vertical colourbar, but is there a way to add text to top and bottom natively in ggplot, other than turning off text in the legend and adding with annotate() (and having to turn clipping off)? What I get What I want I'm sure I'm missing something simple. Code that gives me typical colourbar behaviour: df <- tibble(A = letters[1:5], B = 1:5) ggplot(df, aes(x = A, y = B, fill = B)) + geom_col() + scale_fill_gradient(high = "blue", low = "red", breaks = c(1,5), #labels = letters[1:5], labels = c("low","high") , guide = guide_colorbar( direction = "vertical", title.position = 'top', title.hjust = 0.5, label.hjust = 0.5, #legend.location = "right", label.position = "right") ) + theme(legend.position = "right") I know I can blank out the tick text, and then annotate() "high" and "low" over outside the plotting panel into the legend space, but as I said, is there no "simple" way to swap tick positions to each end of the colourbar?

infoqArticles.title: CNCF Research Shows Virtual Machines Remain Central as AI Workloads Evolve
infoqArticles.description: New research from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Linux Foundation Research finds that VMs host an average of 53% of production applications, while emerging AI and agentic workloads are creating additional demand for virtualisation, particularly where stronger execution isolation is required. By Craig Risi
infoqArticles.author: Craig Risi

infoqArticles.title: OpenAI Scales Git for Coding Agents with Pando
infoqArticles.description: OpenAI has detailed Pando, a new backend that scales Git for concurrent coding-agent workloads without replacing familiar Git workflows. The company reports nearly 80% lower median push latency by coordinating branch updates independently and reusing stored packfiles across fetches. By Eran Stiller
infoqArticles.author: Eran Stiller

infoqArticles.title: Presentation: Inferencing for Enterprises
infoqArticles.description: Dio Rettori discusses the operational realities of enterprise AI inference. Moving beyond fast token generation, he explores why inference requires dedicated systems engineering, tackles GPU utilization pitfalls, compares on-prem versus cloud TCO, and analyzes multi-agent latency determinism. He shares why teams must embed domain ontology directly into models rather than relying solely on RAG. By
infoqArticles.author: Dio Rettori

infoqArticles.title: Article: Engineering Around Non-Determinism: Evals, Grounding, and Release Gates for AI-Drafted Suspicious Reports
infoqArticles.description: Moving GenAI into high-stakes production requires treating non-determinism as an engineering problem. This architectural blueprint shows engineering leaders and architects how to build trustworthy agentic workflows using knowledge graphs, dual-layer eval judges, CI/CD release gates, and regression testing against golden datasets to automate drafting while maintaining zero-hallucination compliance.
infoqArticles.author: Ritesh Modi, Sasidhar Gudala

infoqArticles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Lessons from Building a $100M Product in Six Weeks at OpenAI
infoqArticles.description: At QCon San Francisco 2026, OpenAI's Brian Yang described building the ChatGPT ads product with Codex agents and no human-written code. He outlined layered testing, sandboxes, and batched pull request reviews, and noted failure modes such as code "slop" and unsafe agent actions. He advised gradual adoption and framed engineers as managers of agents. By Daniel Curtis
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Curtis

infoqArticles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: Securing AI Agents in Production
infoqArticles.description: At QCon San Francisco, Google's Amanda Walker framed AI agents as an insider-risk problem operating at machine speed, and described identity, credential and containment patterns for running them safely in production. By Mark Silvester
infoqArticles.author: Mark Silvester

infoqArticles.title: How LinkedIn Built a View-Agnostic Analytics System for Modern iOS UI Architectures
infoqArticles.description: To address the challenge posed by modern iOS UI systems where the logical UI structure may not mirror the native UIKit hierarchy, LinkedIn engineers developed a view-agnostic analytics system build around a shared MeasurableNode contract. By Sergio De Simone
infoqArticles.author: Sergio De Simone

infoqArticles.title: JEP 545 Moves ZGC Memory Preparation off the Startup Path in JDK 28
infoqArticles.description: JEP 545, Faster Startup and Warmup with ZGC, has been integrated into JDK 28, moving heap memory preparation onto concurrent worker threads. ZGC now pre-touches memory as it expands and upgrades small pages to large ones on Linux 6.1 and later, but the 2 MB initial heap behind the JEP's 38% startup and 90% warmup gains requires the adaptive heap sizing flag from JEP 546, which is off by default. B
infoqArticles.author: A N M Bazlur Rahman

infoqArticles.title: Java News Roundup: Java4Shell, Oracle CSPUs, OpenJDK, Azul Payara, BellSoft, Helidon, LangChain4j
infoqArticles.description: This week's Java roundup for November 16th, 2026, features news highlighting: the Java4Shell RCE vulnerability; Oracle CSPUs; Lazy Constants targeted for JDK 28; the November 2026 edition of Azul Payara; point releases of Java Operator SDK, LangChain4j and Micrometer; maintenance releases of Liberica JDK and Helidon; and second release candidates of Hibernate Reactive. By Michael Redlich
infoqArticles.author: Michael Redlich

infoqArticles.title: Netflix at QConSF 2026: Retrofitting the SDLC for AI Coding Agents
infoqArticles.description: At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mark Khuzam of Netflix explained how the Commerce team retrofitted its SDLC so AI coding agents and engineers could ship together. The team wrote 45 architecture decision records for people and agents, added a review agent that posts only verified blockers, and serves per-domain GraphRAG context through a single MCP tool. By Andrew Hoblitzell
infoqArticles.author: Andrew Hoblitzell

infoqArticles.title: Agoda Reduces API Code Review Time by 64% with Modular Architecture
infoqArticles.description: Agoda introduced a modular monolith framework in its post-booking API to reduce coupling without a full rewrite. The platform uses domain components, Data Mapper patterns, typed builders, and ArchUnit tests to enforce boundaries. Framework-backed changes showed 64% shorter median code reviews and 34% faster initial feedback than legacy changes. By Leela Kumili
infoqArticles.author: Leela Kumili

infoqArticles.title: Claude Code Adds Experimental Code Mode to Orchestrate Tool Calls with JavaScript
infoqArticles.description: Anthropic's experimental Code Mode lets Claude Code write JavaScript that chains, parallelizes, and filters Bash, Read, and Edit calls, with changes to how auto mode and hooks review those calls. By Daniel Dominguez
infoqArticles.author: Daniel Dominguez

infoqArticles.title: Podcast: Simulation Can Tell You What Your Agents are Actually Doing: A Conversation with Zhou Yu
infoqArticles.description: Michael Stiefel spoke to Zhou Yu about using dynamic simulations to evaluate AI agents. One particular focus was conversational agents where actions depend on prior responses, and the non-deterministic nation of LLMs means you cannot rely on static, reference-based benchmarks. You need to test them using dynamic simulations that incorporate different personas, goals, and corner cases. By Zhou Yu
infoqArticles.author: Zhou Yu

infoqArticles.title: QCon San Francisco 2026: The Harness Is the New Operating System
infoqArticles.description: At QCon San Francisco 2026, Mad Labs founder and CEO Manju Rajashekhar opened the conference arguing that the harness around an AI model, rather than the model itself, decides what an agent can do and how safely it does it. The keynote mapped the parts of a harness, including context, tools, state, permissions and feedback loops, onto jobs that operating systems already perform. By Andrew Hoblitze
infoqArticles.author: Andrew Hoblitzell

infoqArticles.title: PostgreSQL 19 Released with Online Table Repacking and Query Planning Controls
infoqArticles.description: The PostgreSQL Global Development Group released PostgreSQL 19, introducing changes to database maintenance, query planning, replication, and application development. The release focuses on reducing administrative overhead and improving performance, with new tools for reorganizing tables without downtime and controlling query plans. By Robert Krzaczyński
